def: The fraction of held-out preference pairs on which a reward model scores the chosen response above the rejected one, capped by label noise.
A policy earning a high score from its reward signal by exploiting flaws in the signal, without doing what the signal was meant to measure.
The effect that pushing a policy harder against a learned reward model first raises and then lowers true quality, even as the model's own score keeps rising.
The principle that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure, because optimisation exploits the gap between the measure and what it stands for.
The proxy is the learned reward the optimiser sees; the gold reward is the trusted ground-truth measure used to check what optimisation actually achieved.
Drawing n candidate responses, scoring each with a reward model and returning the highest, a simple way to optimise against a reward without training.
A model's tendency to tell users what they want to hear, such as agreeing with their stated opinion or abandoning a correct answer when challenged.
The tendency of reward models and preference-trained policies to favour longer responses because labellers or surface features correlate length with quality.
A reward model that scores each step of a reasoning chain rather than only the final answer, giving denser but costlier supervision.
Several reward models trained separately whose disagreement or worst-case score is used to make optimisation more conservative.
